title: Small things up close
hook: a leaf, an insect, frost: the world gets bigger the closer you look

segments.voice: Yesterday, one tree: the same tree, every day, for a week, and something ordinary becomes someone you visit. Did you go back for the second visit? What was different? Today we lean in even closer, past the branch, to the leaf. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

A frosted car window on a cold morning. The usual move is to scrape it off and drive. But lean in before the scraper does its work and the frost isn't a white smear at all. It's ferns. Feathers. Tiny branching forests, each one grown in the dark while you slept. The same goes for the vein pattern on a leaf, the legs of a beetle, the rings on a cut onion. Awe is often filed under big things: mountains, oceans, stars. Today it goes the other way. The world gets bigger the closer you look.
screen: `FROST ON A WINDOW.` → `FERNS, FEATHERS, FORESTS.` → `BIGGER THE CLOSER YOU LOOK.`

segments.voice: First, a poet's grain of sand. The English poet William Blake opens his poem Auguries of Innocence with these two lines: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower." Blake isn't saying a grain of sand is pretty. He's saying the whole is folded into the very small, if you have eyes for it. Second, a teacher's flowers. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus points his listeners to the plants at their feet: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." And then he says that Solomon, in all his glory, was not dressed like one of these. A king's robes, outshone by a wild flower. The word is consider. Not glance. Stay with it. Third, why small works. Something huge can overwhelm you; you stand back from it. Something small invites you in. You have to bend down, slow down, get quiet. That posture, low and close and still, is half the practice already. Fourth, what it changes. When you've spent a minute with the veins of one leaf, you can't quite see a whole tree as a green blur again. The detail stays with you. And small things are everywhere: on the windowsill, in the sidewalk crack, on the back of your own hand. You don't need a trip to find awe. You need to bend down.
screen: `BLAKE: A WORLD IN A GRAIN OF SAND.` · `MATTHEW: CONSIDER THE LILIES.` · `SMALL THINGS INVITE YOU IN.` · `YOU DON'T NEED A TRIP. JUST BEND DOWN.` · then, large: `CONSIDER.`

segments.voice: Find one small thing within reach. A leaf, a crumb, a thread on your sleeve, a drop of water on a glass, the skin on the back of your hand. Bring it close, or bring yourself close to it. Look at its edges first. Then its surface. Then whatever lives inside that surface: lines, grains, tiny colors. If your mind wanders, return to one detail. If you pray, you can let this be a way of attending to what's made. If you don't, simply look. The bell holds the time.
Solomon. The king Jesus named when pointing to the lilies of the field, outshone by a wild flower: bend down, look long, and the small thing opens. Today's word.
Your line: up close. Once today, before you brush something aside, a crumb, a bug, a fallen leaf, stop and look at it up close for ten seconds. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Poets, naturalists and contemplatives in several settings practice close looking at small living things; Blake's Auguries of Innocence and Jesus's words about the lilies in Matthew 6 are two texts that point the eye downward.
